catalog_quote: 2.4 A note on tone. Ruruuli-Lunyala is a tonal language: tone is contrastive, i.e. it plays a role in distinguishing lexical items. A comprehensive study of the Ruruuli-Lunyala tone system is underway. The tone bearing unit is the mora (see also de Brito Gottlieb 2019). Preliminary findings suggest that Ruruuli-Lunyala has H, L and Ø tonal values whereby H and L are phonologically activated. Based on the three tone values, several surface tones are realised, they include: HL e.g. kifi [kífì] 'piece of meat (7)', falling contour LH͡LL, e.g. musale [mùsáàlè] 'tree (3)', downstep HH↓ H↓ HL, e.g. busigazi [óβú↓ sí↓ gázì] 'teenage years (14)', downdrift HHL↓ HL, e.g. ómúlà↑ múlì 'judge', and raised low HHH↑ L↓ HL tone ... The falling contour tone is realised on either a long vowel, e.g. [mùsáàlè] 'tree' or a vowel followed by a syllabic nasal, e.g. [kìbáǹja] 'untitled piece of land'.

new_statements.quote: The findings support the argument that Lunyala belongs to the H vs Ø privative tone system with the H as the marked tone. Both the underlying and surface tones are borne by the mora. Underlyingly, the tones pattern as H-Ø, Ø-H-Ø and Ø-Ø in non-augmented nouns and H-Ø and Ø-H-Ø in infinitive verbs. With the L introduced at the surface level, disregarding the variations due to the number and structure of the syllables, the tones broadly pattern as H-L, L-H-L, or L-H in non-augmented nouns, and L-H-L in infinitive verbs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lunyala is described as a privative H vs. Ø (surface H/L) tone language with the mora as tone-bearing unit; the abstract says nothing about word stress or metrical prominence. Whether the thesis body has a stress statement is unknown because the PDF is not accessible.
new_statements.exceptions: none relevant to stress; the abstract mentions OCP-violating tone spreading and falling contours restricted to bimoraic syllables (tonal, not stress-related)
new_statements.identity_note: Kiriggwajjo 2022 describes Lunyala specifically (the Lunyala side of the Ruruuli/Lunyala cluster, JE103, ISO ruc), based on two native-speaker informants, and its abstract explicitly recommends a future comparison with Ruruuli tonology, i.e. the author treats Lunyala and Ruruuli as possibly distinct tonologically. Zellers et al. 2020 treat Ruruuli/Lunyala as one language.

sources.quote: p. 394: 'Ruruuli/Lunyala is a tone language, minimally involving a contrast between high and low tones, with the mora proposed as the tone-bearing unit [7]. ... There is no lexical stress, but it is possible that prominence marking may arise on a phrasal level.' p. 397: 'we find evidence for phrase-final lengthening in both the final and the penultimate syllable nuclei, affecting both short and long vowels' -- i.e. lengthening is an intonation-phrase boundary effect, not word stress.

sources.note: Only source that states the stress fact in so many words ('There is no lexical stress'); instrumental evidence that penultimate/final lengthening is phrasal. Our record's sketch is silent on stress, so this closes the argument-from-silence. downloaded now.
